title: ‘My Hero Academia’ Reworks ‘You Say Run’ Theme With Electric Callboy for 10th Anniversary
description: Toho Co., Ltd. has set a 10th-anniversary version of “You Say Run,” the “My Hero Academia” theme, pairing composer Hayashi Yuki with German band Ele
body:
Toho Co., Ltd. has set a 10th-anniversary version of “You Say Run,” the “My Hero Academia” theme, pairing composer Hayashi Yuki with German band Electric Callboy, with a global release set for Sept. 22.

	The reworked track debuted live at the “My Hero Academia in Concert” show in London on Sept. 20 ahead of the wider rollout. Electric Callboy, known for songs including “Hypa Hypa” and its Babymetal collaboration “Ratatata,” features Kevin Ratajczak and Nico Sallach, who connected with Hayashi after he wrote English lyrics for the anniversary version. Toho’s music team had been looking for international artists who could bring powerful shouts and melodic vocals in keeping with the show’s high-energy tone, which led to the Electric Callboy pairing.
	

	“We are beyond excited to have this opportunity to add our vocals to ‘You Say Run,'” said Ratajczak. “The melody of ‘You Say Run’ is so powerful and uplifting – we just absolutely love this song.”


	Sallach said working on the track was pure fun and a huge honor to collaborate on, adding, “We can’t wait for everyone to hear it! We really hope you’re as excited for it as we are.”

	The new version folds the song’s original orchestral arrangement into Electric Callboy’s blend of EDM and pop hooks, arriving a decade after the anime first premiered. “‘You Say Run,’ one of the signature tracks representing ‘My Hero Academia,’ has been reborn with an unprecedented surge of energy by fusing with the incredible vocals of Electric Callboy,” said Hayashi. “I am deeply honored and thrilled to share this special sound born from the intersection of our shared energy.”
	

	Bones Film also unveiled a new illustration to mark the release, showing Izuku Midoriya (“Deku”) performing a “Smash” in a nod to the cover art of the anime’s original Season 1 soundtrack.

	“I truly hope the song crosses borders and genres, reaches as many hearts as possible, and resonates passionately with everyone,” said Hayashi. “And while the track is absolute perfection, the cover art is top-tier too. Plus Ultra.”

	The release marks a decade since “My Hero Academia” debuted, and the franchise remains among anime’s biggest global hits. Horikoshi Kohei’s manga concluded in August 2024 after selling more than 100 million copies globally, and the anime spans eight seasons, 170+1 episodes and four feature films. The new song is part of the ongoing “My Hero Academia The Animation 10th Anniversary” project, which will continue through 2026 with further announcements on the anniversary’s dedicated website.

	“You Say Run -10th Anniversary Ver.-” by Hayashi Yuki featuring Electric Callboy streams globally and across major platforms starting Sept. 22. 

	“My Hero Academia” is a Japanese anime series based on the manga by Horikoshi Kohei, set in a world where about 80% of the population has a superpowered ability known as a Quirk. It follows Izuku Midoriya and his classmates at U.A. High School as they train to become heroes who protect society from disasters and Quirk-wielding villains. The anime released its eighth and final season in fall 2025.

	Formed in Germany in 2010, Electric Callboy has built a global following on genre-blending hits such as “Hypa Hypa,” “We Got the Moves” and the Babymetal collaboration “Ratatata.” Known for a sound that mixes pop and metalcore, the band is currently building momentum around its new album, “Tanzneid.”

schema.headline: ‘My Hero Academia’ Reworks ‘You Say Run’ Theme With Electric Callboy for 10th Anniversary

title: Ben Affleck Almost Cast Ex-Wife Jennifer Garner in ‘Animals’ Before Deciding ‘We Don’t Wanna Do That’: ‘You Just Get Baggage’
description: Ben Affleck originally wanted to cast his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner, as the leading lady in his latest directorial effort, “Animals,” until a schedul
body:
Ben Affleck originally wanted to cast his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner, as the leading lady in his latest directorial effort, “Animals,” until a scheduling conflict meant he’d have to step into the role opposite her.  

	“I thought, God, Jen Garner would be amazing for this role,” he told Entertainment Weekly. “It also has the added benefit of, like, both of us will see our kids more because we do a week and a week and back and forth. I thought, well, we can coordinate our schedules around it.” He also noted that he thought Garner could “bring something interesting that she hasn’t [done], that I kind of know she can do, that I don’t think she had a chance to do in one movie.” 
	

	Initially, Matt Damon was attached to star as Mark Kimball, the male lead. But because of scheduling conflicts and another film in the same genre slated for a similar release window, Affleck tabled the film two weeks before production was set to begin. When it was time to revive “Animal,” Damon was set to star in another project: “The Odyssey.” 


	“Matt was unfortunately doing another lesser film, obviously, with Odyssey,” Affleck joked. “He chose a smaller director and a smaller film and a smaller role for his career, and I think he’s gonna suffer for it. He’ll regret this choice.” 

	Affleck stepped in for Damon, and the former couple ultimately decided they didn’t want the “baggage” that would come with the on-screen pairing: “I talked to Jen, and she was like, ‘We don’t wanna do that. You just get baggage,’” he said.

	“I would love to work with her, frankly,” he continued. “She’s fabulous, and we’re really good friends, and I’m profoundly grateful to her, and we have a great thing. I still would wanna work with her in the future, but what you don’t wanna do is take the audience’s baggage and have it work against you, you know?”
	

	Co-written by Affleck, Connor O. McIntyre and Billy Ray, “Animals” stars Affleck as a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped, giving him and his wife, Abigail (Kerry Washington), a few hours to come up with the ransom money.

	“Animals” premieres on Oct. 9 on Netflix.

schema.headline: Ben Affleck Almost Cast Ex-Wife Jennifer Garner in ‘Animals’ Before Deciding ‘We Don’t Wanna Do That’: ‘You Just Get Baggage’

title: ‘Angh’ Review: Toronto’s Platform Award Winner Is a Lush Lament for an Indian Tribe in the 1960s
description: Expanding on his 2021 short film, Theja Rio’s debut feature “Angh” forces its way into the hidden crevices between indigenous identity and colonial
body:
Expanding on his 2021 short film, Theja Rio’s debut feature “Angh” forces its way into the hidden crevices between indigenous identity and colonial modernity. This tension unfolds with riveting restraint in a story set in 1960s Nagaland — the eastern Indian state on the Burmese border — following the principled chief of a waning tribe, and the arrival of an American missionary. “Angh” won the top prize in the Platform competition at this year’s Toronto Film Festival, thus qualifying it for the Best International Feature Oscar.
	

	Lush, impenetrable forests play host to the tale of Anghba (Anghlong Konyak), addressed reverentially as “old chief” by his kin who have, willingly or otherwise, been excommunicated. After the death of his wife from disease, his son Amao (Sobino Rengma) — a silent boy searching for his voice — remains the only other member of his Konyak tribe. However, Amao’s curiosity about modern, western clothing and a nearby bustling community of Baptist converts threatens their existence.


	Right from its opening scene, “Angh” frames the arrival of colonial missionaries as a strange, almost alien absurdity. With bow and arrow in hand, Anghba finds his hunt for a wild boar across a riverbank interrupted by a raft floating downstream, as former tribespeople surround a jovial American preacher (Douglas Henshall), much to the chieftain’s chagrin. These impositions are gradual and incredibly well-meaning, although even their medicinal intentions come laced with the word of a foreign lord and savior, whose crucifixes and tales of forgiveness are at odds with the local rituals.
	

	Images often associated with barbarism on screen, like beheading the dead to memorialize them, are approached with an uncanny gentleness. This places the audience alongside the Konyaks, and subverts the traditional, colonial cinematic gaze in the vein of Filipino maestro Lav Diaz. The film’s cast is mostly made up of tribal non-actors, but Anghlong Konyak is its captivating center, as a man whose stubbornness against change sits alongside a lingering grief over his fading way of life.

	The story of the rest of post-independent India lives far away from the film’s peripheries; Rio’s concerns, instead, are hyper-focused on a local tale of transformation and thorny resilience. To the average viewer living in a westernized society, Anghba may come off as obstinate, which feels entirely in tune with the film’s intent. However, his raging protectiveness over what might be lost — language, attire, ritual, even memory — grows more pronounced as Rio veers further into phantasmagoria by way of dreams and visions.

	Together with his cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz, the director crafts an inviting 16mm atmosphere, transforming the textural flaws of celluloid into a living fabric, where dirt, scratches and punctures may as well be insects zipping across the screen, as though this is where the medium belongs. “Angh,” in this way, feels truly alive, and at one with nature — a harmony that’s slowly interrupted as the story unfolds, en route to fiery and devastating conclusions.

	With disarming simplicity, “Angh” challenges closely held notions of default filmic perspectives, offering a whole new world for us to consider through its soulful ruminations, while forcing us to reflect on the cost of our own unassuming norms. It is, in effect, a lament for things which have been lost, a quiet memorial that beats with righteous fury over how easily we let entire ways of life simply slip away — or rather, how we allow them to be snatched in the guise of progress.

schema.headline: ‘Angh’ Review: Toronto’s Platform Award Winner Is a Lush Lament for an Indian Tribe in the 1960s

title: ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny Scores Her Dream Internship in Alexandra Pechman’s Warmly Nostalgic Study of a Bygone Literary Scene
description: In an era when glamorous writing jobs have acquired the unreality of folklore, it feels fitting that Alexandra Pechman’s alluring and affectionate f
body:
In an era when glamorous writing jobs have acquired the unreality of folklore, it feels fitting that Alexandra Pechman’s alluring and affectionate feature debut, “Magazine,” should portray its literary world as a fairy tale. Set in a faraway time — summer 2011 — when office flirtations were fun, ambition was a given and purses hung crossbody, the film follows Nora (Lily McInery), an aspiring poet who lands a competitive internship at Platen, a fictional literary magazine à la The Paris Review. Nora’s time in the office, and the relationships that blossom — and one that withers — over the course of that formative span give shape to this earnest, appealing movie about idealism lost but innocence preserved.
	

	Pechman, who worked in magazines during the era she depicts, drew on her own experiences to write “Magazine.” But the movie — like “Almost Famous” for the n+1 crowd — is less interested in realism than in evoking the shiny, spiky atmosphere of that recent past. Stacked with pitch-perfect needle drops and nods to a sartorial moment, it overflows with warm nostalgia even as it shades its romantic outlook with a shrewd understanding of how it feels to be a young woman in a workplace that inspires reverence while courting disillusion.


	That experience is evergreen and “Magazine” captures its thrills and anxieties with deep affection and sharp attention. The story opens on Nora’s first day of work, as she loiters outside the Platen offices, waiting for the clock to tick a few minutes forward. Thomas (Joshuah Melnick), an assistant editor, has told her to arrive a little after 10 a.m., and when she opens the door five minutes past the hour, she’s confident that the plum (yet naturally unpaid) position awaiting her will be her entry into a rarefied dream career.
	

	At first, the bright, airy Platen offices seem to confirm the fantasy. As appointed by production designer Valeria De Felice, the workspace is a literary dreamscape, lined with Persian rugs and bookcases displaying a rainbow of magazine spines. Skipping inside, Nora joins a cadre of shambling interns whom the editorial staff regard with a mixture of bemusement and disdain. Among them are the self-assured Tabitha (Lukita Maxwell), who, in heeled booties and smudged eyeliner, is clearly a soon-to-be pal, and the curmudgeonly Leonard (Daniel Zolghadri), who can’t resist pointing out that Nora must come from money if she can afford to move to New York for an unpaid role.

	Actually, Nora is living on scholarship funds she won from her unnamed college — but that detail hardly matters. In the mythopoetic world of “Magazine,” money is basically irrelevant. When one coded-wealthy nepotism hire gets fired for neglecting work, the ousting occurs in a passing line of dialogue. And although Thomas — who, as Leonard bitterly notes, has been blessed with good looks and great taste in books — resides in a soaring Manhattan loft owned by his mother, his eventual caddish streak has more to do with his fragile professional ego than his privilege.

	Indeed, in her devotion to sparkle, Pechman declines to probe too deeply into any of the industry’s more hurtful or exploitative dimensions. It’s not that her movie is blind to the hazards; the plot hinges on Nora’s discovery that her bosses aren’t immune to the cliché of hitting on their dewiest interns. But even as she and Tabitha are drawn into such dalliances and then bruised by them, the movie is less interested in passing judgment than in conjuring the freshman thrill of being young, curious and unguarded.

	That can, at points, make “Magazine” seem overly gentle. In its allergy to cynicism, it sometimes comes off like a starry-eyed love story, not between people, but between Nora and the life she has envisioned for herself. As our heroine is drawn deeper into the Platen scene, mingling with haughty editors and attending parties alongside authors of niche renown — one is played by a very funny Alex Edelman — we admire her passion while nervously taking note of her naiveté.

	It’s hardly a surprise when she falls into a relationship with Thomas, whose freckled smirk toggles between mischievous and manipulative. Amiable and self-absorbed in equal measure, he is happy to sleep with Nora so long as nobody finds out and she asks nothing in return. That Thomas has no intention of helping Nora professionally is obvious to us but less so to her, though it is expressed by one of the film’s more unusual and beguiling characters: Daphne (Iris Apatow), a worldly socialite who advises Nora not to have sex with her superiors; they’ll only prove useful if you entice them and then remain out of reach.
	

	That advice — to use one’s femininity to play the players — sounds straight out of Samantha’s mouth in “Sex and the City”: a third-wave theory women can take or leave. Daphne’s strategy is well beyond our naif’s capacity, but in “Magazine,” the sophisticate’s worldview proves apt. As Nora’s feelings for Thomas butt up against her wish for a full-time offer at Platen, her romanticized notions of the people and place come crashing down. As it turns out, the magazine is not an enchanted realm, but a game with particular rules. Nora can either learn to play or walk away.

	“Magazine” is the story of a young woman losing her religion, of youthful certainty clouding with doubt. Pechman brightens Nora’s awakening with notes of optimism: friendships gained, memories forged, lessons learned. There’s no major wreckage here, nor is comeuppance meted out to the wrongdoers. Where other filmmakers might have come down harder on the scene, casting Nora’s experience as evidence of entrenched dysfunction and storm clouds hovering on the horizon, Pechman holds fast to good cheer. But if the movie’s instinct for lenience makes it smaller, it never dims its shine.

schema.headline: ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny Scores Her Dream Internship in Alexandra Pechman’s Warmly Nostalgic Study of a Bygone Literary Scene

title: Barry Keoghan, Joseph Quinn and Harris Dickinson Spotted Filming the Opening of ‘A Hard Day’s Night’ Movie for Beatles Biopic
description: “The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event” stars Barry Keoghan, Joseph Quinn and Harris Dickinson were spotted filming the iconic opening of the “A
body:
“The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event” stars Barry Keoghan, Joseph Quinn and Harris Dickinson were spotted filming the iconic opening of the “A Hard Day’s Night” movie for the forthcoming film, per images via TMZ.

	Directed by Richard Lester, the 1964 film followed the crew over two days as the band struggled to keep themselves and Paul McCartney’s mischievous grandfather in check while preparing for a live TV performance. One of the most notable moments — and the scene apparently being filmed — was a sequence of shots showing the three bandmembers running away from swarps of adoring fans.
	

	Last month, the cast (plus Paul Mescal) were seen recreating the “Abbey Road” album cover for the multi-part biopic. Mescal stars as Paul McCartney, Quinn plays George Harrison, Barry Keoghan portrays Ringo Starr and Harris Dickinson plays John Lennon.


	Each of the four films will focus on a different member of the band. “Each man has his own story, but together they are legendary,” reads the official logline.

	In addition to the main bandmembners, other cast members include Saoirse Ronan as Linda McCartney, James Norton as Brian Epstein, Mia McKenna-Bruce as Maureen Starkey, Anna Sawai as Yoko Ono, Aimee Lou Wood as Pattie Boyd, Harry Lloyd as George Martin, David Morrissey as Jim McCartney, Leanne Best as Mimi Smith, Bobby Schofield as Neil Aspinall, Daniel Hoffmann-Gill as Mal Evans, Arthur Darvill as Derek Taylor and Adam Pally as Allen Klein.

	As previously reported by Variety, all four of the films will be released theatrically in April 2028.

schema.headline: Barry Keoghan, Joseph Quinn and Harris Dickinson Spotted Filming the Opening of ‘A Hard Day’s Night’ Movie for Beatles Biopic

title: Apple TV Finally Schedules Jessica Chastain-Led Thriller ‘The Savant’
description: After having pulled the topical Jessica Chastain-led thriller “The Savant” on Sept. 23, 2025 — just days before its premiere — Apple TV has confirme
body:
After having pulled the topical Jessica Chastain-led thriller “The Savant” on Sept. 23, 2025 — just days before its premiere — Apple TV has confirmed it will finally release the show a year and a half later — in Spring 2027, notably after November’s midterm elections.

	The company had gotten cold feet about “The Savant” after the 2025 assassination of far-right activist Charlie Kirk, and released an opaque statement at the time, saying: “After careful consideration, we have made the decision to postpone ‘The Savant.’ We appreciate your understanding and look forward to releasing the series at a future date.”
	

	The next day, Chastain — who is an executive producer of “The Savant,” as well as its star — released a statement in which she vehemently disagreed with the company’s decision, arguing that while she values her partnership with Apple, “we’re not aligned on the decision to pause the release of ‘The Savant.'”


	“In the last five years since we’ve been making the show, we’ve seen an unfortunate amount of violence in the United States: the kidnapping attempt on Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer; the January 6th attack on the Capitol; the assassination attempts on President Trump; the political assassinations of Democratic representatives in Minnesota; the attack on Speaker Pelosi’s husband; the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk; the recent shooting at an ABC affiliate station in California; and over 300 school shootings across this country,” Chastain wrote on Instagram on Sept. 24, 2025. “These incidents, though far from encompassing the full range of violence witnessed in the United States, illustrate a broader mindset that crosses the political spectrum and must be confronted. I’ve never shied away from difficult subjects, and while I wish this show wasn’t so relevant, unfortunately it is.
	

	“‘The Savant’ is about the heroes who work every day to stop violence before it happens, and honoring their courage feels more urgent than ever,” Chastain’s statement continued. “While I respect Apple’s decision to pause the release for now, I remain hopeful the show will reach audiences soon. Until then, I’m wishing safety and strength for everyone, and I’ll let you know if and when ‘The Savant’ is released.”

	In “The Savant,” Chastain plays Jodi Goodwin, a veteran, wife and mother whose job is to infiltrate online forums in which white supremacists gather and sometimes plan domestic terror attacks. Creator Melissa James Gibson adapted “The Savant” from a 2019 Cosmopolitan story by Andrea Stanley titled “Is It Possible to Stop a Mass Shooting Before It Happens?”

	The day Apple pulled the show, Variety TV critic Aramide Tinubu argued that the company was making a mistake, and wrote the decision was “another chilling example of how business giants are running scared of the Trump administration, and bowing to pressure before it even exists.”

	And eight days after Apple postponed “The Savant,” FBI Director Kash Patel announced he was killing the agency the Chastain character worked for, announcing the act on X. He wrote: “James Comey wrote ‘love letters’ to the ADL and embedded FBI agents with them — a group that ran disgraceful ops spying on Americans. That era is OVER. This FBI won’t partner with political fronts masquerading as watchdogs.”

	Since “The Savant” was pulled last year, the fate of the series has been an ongoing question. The show continued to live on Apple TV’s press site, but with no information on when — or if — it would ever air. Earlier this year, Apple TV insiders suggested that the premiere of “The Savant” would take place this winter or early spring, tied to other shows with female leads — either Season 2 of “The Last Thing He Told Me” in February 2026, or in March, paired with “Imperfect Women.” But those shows’ launches came and went without any sign of “The Savant.”

	In April, Chastain told Variety that “The Savant” would finally get a premiere date: “Before it was like, ‘I don’t know if we’re going to see it,’ but now I can say, ‘We’re going to see it,” Chastain told Variety‘s Marc Malkin exclusively at the Breakthrough Prize ceremony in Santa Monica. At that time, sources told Malkin that “The Savant” would premiere this July. Then that date came and went as well.
	

	Ultimately, the sense was that Apple TV wouldn’t premiere “The Savant” until after the midterm elections, despite the fact that the show would probably have little impact on the nation’s political races. Nonetheless, that is apparently what Apple TV decided. Meanwhile, Apple TV’s website still promises that “The Savant” is “coming soon” — in 2025.

	Deadline was the first to report that Apple TV is slating “The Savant” for release.

schema.headline: Apple TV Finally Schedules Jessica Chastain-Led Thriller ‘The Savant’

title: NYU Langone Privately Bought the Site of a Landmark AMC Theater — New Yorkers Are Now Fighting to Save It
description: “We came to this place for magic.”On a rainy Sunday afternoon, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal stood in solidarity with more than 100
body:
“We came to this place for magic.”On a rainy Sunday afternoon, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal stood in solidarity with more than 100 New Yorkers outside AMC Kips Bay 15. In his best Australian accent, he recited Nicole Kidman’s iconic AMC Theatres ad in a loving tribute to the neighborhood’s longstanding cultural institution. But despite a record-breaking summer at the box office, the Kips Bay multiplex is expected to close at the end of this year.


	“I’m a lifelong resident of Kips Bay, and I came out here to support my favorite theater that I’ve been going to since I was a child,” said Lucy Di Lorenzo, one of the many Gen-Zers who attended the protest.
	

	The site of the Kips Bay AMC, the chain’s second-largest multiplex in Manhattan, was privately purchased by NYU Langone over a year ago. But several city officials at the protest told Variety they didn’t learn about the deal until after it had gone through.

	“NYU is a neighbor, and we’ve worked with them in many different capacities, so it was surprising that we had to reach out to them to find out that they were the ones looking to acquire the land behind us,” New York State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez explained after the protest. “It’s not unreasonable to ask NYU to be proactive in engaging with the community.”

	The “Save the Kips Bay AMC Theater Rally” was organized by the Eleanor Roosevelt Independent Democrats, a local political club representing several communities across the Lower East Side, East Village and Midtown East. Judith Gross, the group’s president, says her members are “devastated” by the news but remain hopeful they can get through to AMC Theatres and NYU Langone.

	“I’m hoping AMC and NYU see what we’ve done here,” Gross said. “This neighborhood is not a campus for NYU and its medical offices. We’re guiding the whole community to protest these takeovers of what little community space we have left.”
	

	Several local businesses have joined Gross’ rallying cry, including Paddy Reilly’s Music Bar, the staple Irish pub located just around the corner from AMC Kips Bay. After promoting the protest on social media, the bar offered a free drink to anyone who came in afterward with a selfie from the rally.

	“It’s very important because we have a lot of young people in this neighborhood who love to go to the movie theater,” said Desi Murray, who has owned Paddy Reilly’s for the past three years. “It would be a big loss for the community.”

	Paddy Reilly’s is celebrating its 40th year in business. Inside the bar, several locals mourned the potential loss of a community gathering space that’s been around even longer.

	“We’ve been here since ’73,” a patron named Cesar told his buddies at the bar. He took a sip of Guinness. “There has always been a theater here.”As the pub-goers clamored over how surprisingly funny “Resident Evil” was and how great Robert Pattinson’s Batman is, the fate of their favorite local movie theater remains in limbo. It’s a conflict playing out on a much larger scale with the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, which many of Hollywood’s most prominent voices are arguing would diminish opportunities and resources for creatives.

	“And right here, the same thing is happening,” Gonzalez explained. “We’re getting a big new partner coming in, potentially kicking this out, limiting options to see the movies in our neighborhood. And all we’re asking for, whether it’s in Hollywood or right here in Pittsburgh, is for everyday people to be included and have our voices heard.”In a statement to Variety, NYU Langone has responded to the protests: “NYU Langone is committed to providing high-quality, accessible healthcare to the communities we serve. We have been exploring opportunities to expand clinical services and improve access to care as we continue to see growing demand at our Manhattan campus.When the owner of the Second Avenue property approached us most recently regarding a potential sale, we recognized that the site’s proximity to our hospital could help support those long-term community healthcare needs. The purchase remains under contract and is not expected to close until early next year. Years before NYU Langone was approached about the property, AMC and the landlord entered into a lease granting either party a right to terminate at any time.We will provide updates on our clinical plans when the transaction is finalized.”

schema.headline: NYU Langone Privately Bought the Site of a Landmark AMC Theater — New Yorkers Are Now Fighting to Save It

title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Cancellation: Creator, Stars JoAnna Garcia Swisher and Jamie Lynn Spears React to Netflix Series Ending
description: Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, stars Jamie Lynn Spears, JoAnna Garcia Swisher and creator and showrunner Sh
body:
Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, stars Jamie Lynn Spears, JoAnna Garcia Swisher and creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson are looking back on the romantic drama’s 5 Season run.

	Under an Instagram post featuring behind-the-scenes and on-set snaps of the show, Swisher wrote a lengthy caption about her feelings surrounding the show’s ending.


	“How do you say goodbye to something that became so much more than a job? Seven years. Five seasons. A million tiny moments that somehow became a whole life,” she began. “‘Sweet Magnolias’ came into my world during a chapter that held some of my deepest loss and, somehow, some of my greatest joy. I lost both of my parents during those early seasons, and in a time when I wasn’t always sure how to keep moving forward, Serenity gave me somewhere to go. These people gave me somewhere to belong.”
	

	She continued: “To every single person who made this show, and every single person who watched it, loved it, shared it, and found a little piece of themselves in Serenity…thank you. You will never fully know what you gave me.”

	Jamie Lynn Spears, who played Noreen Fitzgibbons in the show, wrote on Instagram that she “can’t put into words how much the people who make up our Sweet Mags family mean to me, and that’s not just the producers, cast, crew, & @Netflix who are like actual family at this point, but also each of you who watched and became a part of our family as well.”

	“I was given the gift of being able to provide for my family, doing something I was proud of, surrounded by people I respected and loved while creating something we all valued,” she concluded. “I owe it all to each and every person who loved Serenity, and the people who made it what it was, Thank you, Thank you, Thank you, I’m so grateful to be a part of this magical family and that’s something that will never end🤍🤍”
	

	Anderson also shared her reflections in an Instagram post Saturday. “Living in Serenity for five seasons has been a privilege and a blessing,” she wrote. “The people I’ve met and worked with — our incredible writers, cast, crew, executives, and producers — have touched my heart and changed my life.”

	“And our fans have been amazing in their passion for our characters. Thank you all. Though our journey has sadly come to an end, I hope Serenity will always have a place in your heart. Keep pouring it out!”

	The Netflix show first premiered on the platform in May 2020, and starred Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley. Originally adapted from the book series by New York Times best-selling author Sherryl Woods, the streamer announced that the show continuously ranked among Netflix’s Global Top 10 in over 60 countries after announcing its return for a fifth season in 2025.

	The “comfort drama,” as described by Netflix, followed the lifelong friendship between Maddie (Swisher), Dana Sue (Elliott), and Helen (Headley) “as they juggle relationships, family and careers in the charming small town of Serenity, S.C.”

	Though “Sweet Magnolias” may be coming to an end, Netflix announced that Swisher and Anderson would be teaming for a new drama series titled “Ladies of the House.”

	Variety previously reported that Anderson will serve as showrunner, with Swisher potentially starring and executive producing with Kate Gordon under their Rolling Clover banner, alongside executive producers at Black Label Media.

	The logline reads, “When the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.”

schema.headline: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Cancellation: Creator, Stars JoAnna Garcia Swisher and Jamie Lynn Spears React to Netflix Series Ending

title: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Review: A Riveting South Korean Popcorn Thriller About a Real Assassination
description: Hur Jin-ho’s star-studded “The Assassin(s)” turns the holes in a public investigation into an imaginative mystery along the lines of Oliver Stone’s
body:
Hur Jin-ho’s star-studded “The Assassin(s)” turns the holes in a public investigation into an imaginative mystery along the lines of Oliver Stone’s “JFK.” Like Stone’s provocative thriller, Hur crafts a clockwork political saga sure to spark curiosities about the attempted assassination of strongman South Korean prime minister Park Chung-hee in 1974, which resulted in the death of his wife, first lady Yuk Young-soo, as well as a young bystander.
	

	The film ties these events into larger concerns surrounding freedom of the press and some inventive government conspiracies. Your mileage may vary when it comes to the extent of these fabrications, even though “The Assassin(s)” begins with a disclaimer hinting at its own fictions. Regardless, its drama is solid and propulsive, beginning with a group of journalists being harangued by the KCIA (Korean Central Intelligence Agency) for publishing troublesome investigations en route to the botched assassination (intentionally so, according to the film’s internal logic). 

	The three most prominent characters are charismatic and sympathetic in equal measure. Two of them are journalists at the Dong-sung Daily, who mount a heroic stand against government forces at a time of severe censorship. Fiery rookie Young-il (Lee Min-ho) — the younger brother of a connected official — is assigned to cover the prime minister’s Liberation Day speech when the shooting goes awry, leading him to witness the events first-hand. The older, world-weary Jae-hwan (Park Hae-il) leads the City Desk, and investigates the event from a distance with the help of his police source, diligent detective Cheol-goo (Yoo Hai-jin). 
	

	The local policeman isn’t just present on the day, but tries to stop the eventual assassin from entering the auditorium for the prime minister’s speech, until he’s directed otherwise by senior authorities. He’s punished regardless by suits who refuse to listen, galvanizing the characters’ investigations into a larger collusion.

	With a murderer’s row of supporting actors — like Park Hoon as a vicious KCIA goon harassing the Dong-sung workers, and Bae Seong-woo as the paper’s editor, trapped between maintaining journalistic integrity and bowing to censorious demands — the film establishes and unravels its drama at lightning speed. Hur judiciously constructs scene after scene that pulls and pushes the various probes closer to and further from the mysterious truth, which feels at once obscured and hidden in plain sight. As the puzzle pieces shift slowly into place, these revelations are jaw-dropping (once again, in their highly fictitious context), leading to a journalistic urgency.

	Like any good cover-up movie, “The Assassin(s)” luxuriates in process and proficiency, following its cops and journalists sleuthing about to ask questions and peek at documents, poking their noses where they shouldn’t. It’s an invigorating kind of cinema, and Hur knows exactly how and when to tighten the screws, bringing his characters face to face with critical dangers, and with identities shrouded in mystery. These unspool in the form of action scenes where the stakes aren’t just personal safety, but the larger ideals of a nation under political suppression. Its tale of a Zainichi assassin (an ethnic Korean in Japan), as well as fraying political tensions between the North and South, take its characters far and wide, in a follow-the-money treasure hunt dangerously close to the halls of power.

	To spin total concoctions into something so riveting is — for better or worse — an admirable cinematic skill, one Hur uses to turn a tale of forensic malfeasance into mass entertainment of considerable quality. (At Toronto, where the film premiered, it was the second runner-up for the International People’s Choice Award.) There are unanswered questions about these events to this day, and while “The Assassin(s)” isn’t the answer anyone was looking for, the movie taps into a national mood of frustrated anti-authoritarianism, while playing melodramatic tribute to those willing to speak truth to power. The result is rousing, popcorn-munching fun.

schema.headline: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Review: A Riveting South Korean Popcorn Thriller About a Real Assassination

title: Jhené Aiko Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Westside Whimsy’
description:
Jhené Aiko has scored her first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 with her fourth record “Westside Whimsy.”

	Aiko bows atop the chart with 74,000 eq
body:
Jhené Aiko has scored her first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 with her fourth record “Westside Whimsy.”

	Aiko bows atop the chart with 74,000 equivalent album units, making it the first R&B album by a woman to top the Billboard 200 this year and the first to reach No. 1 since SZA’s “SOS” in May 2025. This year, the only other R&B album to hit No. 1 was Bruno Mars’ “The Romantic.”


	“Westside Whimsy,” which touts features from Kendrick Lamar, Tyga and Larry June, arrived without much notice after Aiko announced the project less than a week before its release. It marks her sixth album to hit the Billboard 200, dating back to her first entry, “Sail Out,” in 2013. She last released her third album “Chilombo” in 2020, which debuted at No. 2 and earned three Grammy nominations including album of the year, best progressive R&B album and best R&B performance for “Lightning & Thunder.”
	

	Aiko’s latest is the only album this week to debut in the Billboard 200 top 10. Ella Langley, who is expected to achieve the longest-running No. 1 on the Hot 100 tomorrow with “Choosin’ Texas,” falls to No. 2 with “Dandelion,” moving roughly 60,000 equivalent album units. Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” comes in at No. 3, followed by Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem” at No. 4 and Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide” at No. 5.

	Rounding out spots six through 10 are Drake’s “Iceman,” Ariana Grande’s “Petal,” Rod Wave’s “Don’t Look Down,” Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” and Kahan’s “Stick Season.”

title: Man Jumps Overboard Off Carnival Cruise Ship
description:
Carnival Cruise
                          Man Jumps Overboard, Ship Turns Around to Search
body:
Carnival Cruise
                          Man Jumps Overboard, Ship Turns Around to Search
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 20, 2026
                            10:43 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 20, 2026
                                11:48 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A Carnival Cruise ship made a U-turn to search for a man who jumped overboard into the waters off Mexico ... and one of the passengers taking the trip told TMZ all about the tragic event.
      
    
            The search began on Saturday morning as the ship was heading along the coast of Mexico's Baja peninsula.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A rep for Carnival tells TMZ ... "Carnival Cruise Line confirmed Saturday that a male guest aboard Carnival Panorama jumped overboard while the ship was sailing from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico to Long Beach, California."
      

            When they were notified that a guest was missing, the crew reviewed CCTV footage as part of their investigation and alerted both the U.S. and Mexico Coast Guards.
      
    
            The cruise line added ... "Carnival is providing support to the family who was traveling with the guest, and our thoughts and prayers are with them and their loved ones."
      
    
            A passenger tells TMZ ... the incident occurred in the waters along the Baja peninsula as the ship was returning to Long Beach.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The cruise ship guest added ... a family member had guest services page the missing passenger around 10:30 AM after searching for him.
      
    
            After CCTV footage confirmed he went overboard, the ship turned back around at 2 PM to search before resuming its route to Long Beach at approximately 4:30 PM ... the passenger says.
      
    
            We've asked Carnival Cruise Line and the U.S. Coast Guard about the status of the man who jumped overboard ... so far, no word back.
